title: Design a distributed rate limiter
summary: Per-key limits shared by many gateway nodes: where the limiter sits, the sliding window counter, atomic Redis scripts, fail-open versus fail-closed and the headers callers need.

steps.title: Requirements and estimates
body: **The ask:** every API key gets a limit (say 100 requests per second, or 10,000 per hour) and every gateway node
must enforce the **same** limit, however many nodes there are.
| Kind | Requirement |
| Functional | limits per API key, per user or per IP, per route; reject with `429 Too Many Requests` and `Retry-After` |
| Non-functional | adds under 1-2 ms to each request; a limiter outage must not take the API down; roughly accurate is fine (a few % over is acceptable) |
| Out of scope | billing, quotas measured in days (use a usage pipeline, not the hot path) |
```text
peak traffic      50,000 requests / s across 40 gateway nodes
limiter calls     one atomic round trip per request = 50,000 ops / s   (a few Redis shards handle that)
keys              1 M active API keys x 2 windows x ~100 bytes   ≈ 200 MB of memory
latency budget    same-AZ round trip to Redis ≈ 0.2-0.5 ms
The numbers say: memory is trivial, **one network round trip per request** is the real cost, and it must be
atomic or concurrent nodes will both let request 101 through.

steps.prompt: Where does the shared limiter usually sit, and why?
options: In the API gateway (or edge proxy), before the request reaches any service, so rejected requests cost almost nothing
Inside each backend service, so each team can tune it
In the database, as a trigger that counts inserts
In the client SDK, so the server never has to check
steps.explain: Rejecting at the edge is cheapest and protects everything behind it. Services may still keep their own coarse limits (a bulkhead for their own database), but the per-customer contract lives at the gateway. A client-side limiter is a politeness, never protection.

steps.title: The sliding window counter
body: Module 8 covers the algorithms in depth. The one most shared limiters use is the **sliding window counter**:
keep a count for the current fixed window and the previous one, and weight the previous one by how much of it
still overlaps the sliding window.
```text
previous window (1 s)          current window (1 s)
80 requests      ^ 25% in      30 so far
<------ sliding 1 s window ------>
estimate = previous x (1 - elapsed / window) + current
= 80 x 0.75 + 30 = 90        allow while estimate < limit
Two integers per key, no list of timestamps, and no burst of 2 x limit at the window edge that a plain fixed
window allows. It assumes the previous window's requests were spread evenly, which is close enough in practice.

code: var estimate = prev * (1 - elapsed / window) + curr;
steps.explain: A quarter of the current window has passed, so three quarters of the previous window still overlap: 80 x 0.75 = 60, plus the 30 already counted.

steps.title: Atomic in Redis: one script, one round trip
body: `GET` then `SET` from the gateway is a race: two nodes both read 99, both allow, both write 100. Make the
read-check-write **one atomic operation** on the server. Redis runs a Lua script atomically (nothing else
runs on that shard meanwhile), and it is one round trip:
```lua
-- KEYS[1] = rl:{key42}:1732700000   ARGV[1] = limit   ARGV[2] = window in ms
local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
if n == 1 then
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
end
if n > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
return 1
- Load it once with `SCRIPT LOAD` and call it with `EVALSHA` (Redis 7+ also has `FUNCTION LOAD` and `FCALL`).
- In a **Redis Cluster**, every key one script touches must be in the same hash slot: put the shared part in
braces, `rl:{key42}:...`, so the current and previous window of one API key land together.
- The expiry cleans up old windows, so memory stays bounded.

steps.prompt: Complete the fixed-window script: count the request, and give the key an expiry only when the window starts.
code: if n > tonumber(ARGV[1]) then return 0 end
steps.explain: `INCR` creates the key at 1 if it is missing and returns the new value atomically. `PEXPIRE` takes milliseconds (`EXPIRE` takes seconds). Setting the expiry only on the first request keeps the window fixed instead of sliding forward on every call.

steps.prompt: Redis is unreachable for 30 seconds. Should the limiter fail **open** (allow) or **closed** (reject)?
items: Sending SMS one-time codes (each one costs money)
Free-tier AI image generation on expensive GPUs
steps.explain: Fail open when the limiter only protects fairness and the backends can take a short spike; fail closed when abuse costs money or security (brute force, SMS pumping fraud). Many teams fail open but fall back to a coarse local in-memory limit per node, so it is never unlimited.

prompt: **Symptom first.** A customer on the 100 requests/second plan is measured at about 400 requests/second, all
returning 200. You run 4 gateway nodes behind a round-robin load balancer. The limiter config is:
options: Each node keeps its own bucket, so the real limit is 100 x 4 nodes. Use a shared store (or divide the limit by the node count and accept the error)
The token bucket allows bursts of 4 x the rate
Round robin is sending all of that customer's traffic to one node
The customer is retrying 429s, which counts as 200s
steps.explain: An in-memory limiter is per process. With N nodes you get N x the limit. A shared counter (Redis) fixes it; `rate / N` per node is a cheap approximation that drifts when nodes scale or traffic is uneven.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: running a rate limiter
steps.body: The commands you reach for when the limiter is slow, wrong or the reason customers are angry.

toolkit.what: Loads a Lua script once and returns its SHA1, so callers send the short hash instead of the whole script.
flags: upload the script, print its sha
run it: 1 is the number of keys that follow
check it is still cached (it is lost on restart: retry with EVAL on NOSCRIPT)
toolkit.when: deploying or testing a new limiter script

toolkit.what: Measures round-trip latency to Redis continuously: the floor of what the limiter adds to each request.
flags: min, max and average in ms, updated live
a new line every 15 s, to spot spikes
toolkit.when: gateway p99 rose and you suspect the limiter

toolkit.what: Per-command call counts and microseconds per call, so you see whether EVALSHA got slower or busier.
flags: zero the counters before a test

toolkit.what: Shows which hash slot a key maps to, to check that one key's windows share a slot (a script fails with CROSSSLOT otherwise).
flags: a hash tag: only the part in braces is hashed

toolkit.what: Calls the API until it is limited and shows the status and the headers a caller needs to back off.
flags: seconds (or a date) to wait before retrying
remaining quota headers from the IETF draft; many APIs use X-RateLimit-* instead
toolkit.example: for i in $(seq 1 120); do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H 'X-Api-Key: test-key' https://api.example.com/v1/search?q=lamp; done | sort | uniq -c

steps.prompt: Match each command to what it tells you.
pairs: runs the loaded limiter script for one key
how much one round trip to Redis costs, over time
calls and microseconds per call for each command
which hash slot a key lives in
how long a limited caller should wait

steps.title: A sliding window counter
prompt: Write a class `SlidingWindowCounter` (what the Redis script computes, with time passed in so it can be tested):
- `SlidingWindowCounter(int limit, long windowMs)`: a limit or window of `0` or less throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- `bool Allow(string key, long nowMs)`: windows are aligned: the current one starts at `nowMs / windowMs * windowMs`.
When time has moved into the **next** window, the old current count becomes the previous count; if it moved
further than that, the previous count is `0`. Then
`estimate = previous x (1 - (nowMs - currentStart) / windowMs) + current` (as a `double`). If `estimate < limit`
the request is allowed and counted; otherwise it is rejected and **not** counted.
- Each key has its own counts.
With a limit of 10 per 1,000 ms: 10 requests at t = 100 pass and the 11th fails. At t = 1,500 the previous 10
still count half, so 5 more pass.
starter: public bool Allow(string key, long nowMs) => true;
solution: readonly Dictionary<string, (long Start, int Current, int Previous)> state = new();
public bool Allow(string key, long nowMs)
else if (s.Start != start) s = (start, 0, start - s.Start == windowMs ? s.Current : 0);
hints: Keep `(long Start, int Current, int Previous)` per key in a dictionary.
When `start` changed: if `start - old.Start == windowMs` the old current becomes previous, else previous is 0. Then compute the weight `1.0 - (nowMs - start) / (double)windowMs`.

Dojo.Eq("10 of 12 allowed in the first window", 10, dojoFirst);
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < 10; dojoI++) if (dojoL.Allow("a", 1500)) dojoMid++;
Dojo.Eq("half-way into the next window the previous 10 weigh 5: 5 more pass", 5, dojoMid);
Dojo.Eq("another key has its own window", true, dojoL.Allow("b", 1500));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < 12; dojoI++) if (dojoL.Allow("a", 3000)) dojoLate++;
Dojo.Eq("two windows later the old counts are gone", 10, dojoLate);
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < 12; dojoI++) if (dojoC.Allow("c", 1850)) dojoEnd++;
